items: Read a short picture book together and pause twice to ask, "What do you think about that?"
Play "Simon says" with three or four instructions and swap so your child gives some too.
Read a story and ask your child to do an action whenever a certain word comes up, like clapping for "bear".
After a page, invite your child to ask you one question about the picture or the story.
Listen to everyday sounds on a walk and talk about what each one might be.
Tell your child a short story about your day and ask them to tell you one thing they noticed.
Read a page, then ask, "Is there anything you want to know more about?"
Give a slightly muddled instruction on purpose and praise your child for asking what you meant.
After a story, take turns saying your favourite part and why.
Look at a picture in a book together and each ask one "I wonder…" question about it.
At a mealtime, ask an open question like "What was the best bit of today?" and keep chatting for three turns each.
Play shops with toys, taking turns to be the shopkeeper and customer.
Use a pretend phone and have a back-and-forth chat about a made-up trip.
On a walk, take turns pointing something out and saying one thing about it.
Pass a soft toy back and forth, and only the person holding it talks, then hands it over for a reply.
Pick a new word from a book this week, like "enormous", and both try to use it in a sentence today.
Ask your child for their idea on what to have for lunch and why.
Build a tower together and take turns suggesting how to make it taller.
Play "What could this be?" with a cardboard tube, sharing ideas like a telescope or a tunnel.
Plan a teddy bears' picnic together, letting your child suggest the food and games.
Put an ice cube in a bowl and ask your child to explain why it is getting smaller.
On a walk, look at puddles or wet leaves and ask, "Why do you think it is wet here?"
Drop a toy and a feather together and ask your child why one landed first.
Read a story and ask why a character felt sad or happy.
Watch the plants or trees on a windy day and ask why they are moving.
At bedtime, ask your child to tell you something they did today, starting with "Today I…".
Ask what they would like to do tomorrow and help them say it with "Tomorrow I will…".
Look at an old photo together and ask your child to tell you what happened, using "and" or "because".
Ask how they are feeling right now and help them finish "I feel… because…".
Play a game where you start a sentence with "I was happy when…" and your child finishes it.
After reading a story, ask your child to tell it back to you using a few toys as the characters.
Draw three quick boxes and help your child draw the beginning, middle and end of a story.
Ask your child to retell a favourite fairy tale to a teddy.
Read a story and later in the day ask, "Can you tell me what happened in that story?"
Act out a well-known story like "The Three Billy Goats Gruff" together, with your child telling it.
In "Goldilocks and the Three Bears", what do you think the bears will find when they come home?
e.g. Their porridge eaten, a broken chair and Goldilocks asleep in bed.
In "The Three Little Pigs", what will happen when the wolf blows on the straw house?
It will fall down.
What will happen when the wolf gets to the brick house?
He can't blow it down.
In "The Gingerbread Man", what do you think the fox will do?
e.g. Trick him and eat him.
If a story character plants a magic bean, what might happen next?
e.g. It grows into a giant beanstalk.
What does "enormous" mean?
Very, very big.
What does "tiny" mean?
Very, very small.
If a character is "exhausted", how do they feel?
Very tired.
What does it mean if someone "whispers"?
They talk very quietly.
What is a "nest" for?
e.g. A home a bird makes for its eggs and babies.
What sound does the letter m make?
"mmm"
What sound do the letters s and h make together?
"sh"
What sound do c and h make together?
"ch"
What sound does the letter t make?
"t" (a short sound, not "tuh")
What sound do two o's make together, like in "moon"?
"oo"
Blend these sounds: c – a – t. What word is it?
cat
Blend these sounds: s – u – n. What word is it?
sun
Blend these sounds: d – o – g. What word is it?
dog
Blend these sounds: sh – i – p. What word is it?
ship
Blend these sounds: ch – i – p. What word is it?
chip
Can you read this: "I can hop."
I can hop.
Can you read this: "the cat is on the mat"
the cat is on the mat
Which tricky word is this: "the"?
the
Can you read this: "a big red bus"
a big red bus
Can you read this: "I see a dog."
I see a dog.
Practise writing the first letter of your child's name in a tray of flour or sand with a finger.
Draw big letters in the air together, saying where to start each one.
Write letters with chalk on the pavement or with a wet paintbrush on a wall outside.
Make letter shapes out of playdough snakes and trace them with a finger.
Write a short shopping list together, with your child writing the first letter of each item.
What sounds can you hear in "pig"?
p – i – g
What sounds can you hear in "sat"?
s – a – t
What sounds can you hear in "hen"?
h – e – n
What sounds can you hear in "fish"?
f – i – sh
What letters would you write for "red"?
r, e, d
Help your child write a label for a drawing, like "my cat".
Write a short note together to leave for someone at home, such as "I love you".
Make a simple card and help your child write "to Mum" or "to Dad" inside.
Ask your child to write one short sentence about their day, like "I went to the park".
Make a sign for a toy shop game, such as "shop is open".
If you have 5 sweets in one hand and none in the other, how many altogether?
What two numbers can make 6?
e.g. 3 and 3, or 4 and 2, or 5 and 1
What number is one more than 7?
What number is one less than 10?
I have 8 grapes and you have 8 grapes. Do we have the same?
Yes, the same
Hold up 3 fingers quickly: how many did you see without counting?
Roll a dice: how many dots, without counting them?
The number of dots shown, e.g. 4
Put 2 spoons on the table for a second: how many?
Show 5 fingers on one hand quickly: how many?
Clap 4 times: how many claps did you hear?
What is 2 add 3?
What is 4 take away 1?
What is double 3?
What goes with 7 to make 10?
What is double 5?
What number comes after 19?
What number comes after 20?
Can you count from 18 to 23?
What number comes after 29?
What number comes before 22?
I have 4 cars and you have 6 cars. Who has more?
You do (6 is more than 4)
A plate has 3 biscuits and another has 3 biscuits. Are they the same?
Yes, the same
Which is fewer, 7 apples or 2 apples?
2 apples
Which is bigger, 9 or 5?
Sam has 8 blocks and Mia has 10. Who has fewer?
Sam
If you share 6 grapes between 2 people, how many does each get?
Is 4 an odd or an even number?
Even
Is 7 an odd or an even number?
Odd
What is double 4?
Share 10 raisins between 2 teddies: how many each?
What does the prefix 'mis-' mean in 'misbehave'?
Badly or wrongly – to behave badly.
If 'super-' means above or more than, what might 'superstar' mean?
A star who is more than ordinary – a really famous star.
What is the root word in 'unhappily'?
happy
What does 'anti-' mean in 'anticlockwise'?
Against or opposite – going the opposite way to a clock's hands.
What does 'sub-' tell you about where a submarine goes?
Under – it goes under the sea.
Which letter is silent in 'island'?
The 's'.
Which letters make the 'ar' sound in 'heart'?
The 'ea' (h-e-a-r-t).
Which letter is silent at the start of 'knowledge'?
The 'k'.
In 'women', which letter makes an 'i' sound in the first part?
The 'o' – it's said 'wim-in'.
What sound do the letters 'eigh' make in 'eight' and 'weight'?
An 'ay' sound.
Read a short poem or a bit of a play script aloud together, then perform it with actions and loud, quiet or scared voices.
Ask your child to retell a fairy tale or myth they know in their own words, with a clear beginning, middle and end.
When you meet an unfamiliar word while reading, look it up together in a dictionary and use it in a new sentence.
Pick a favourite sentence or phrase from today's reading and talk about why it grabs your interest.
Compare two stories you've read and talk about what they have in common, such as good against evil or a magic object.
Ben hid his face and went red when everyone clapped – how did he feel, and how do you know?
e.g. Embarrassed or shy – because he hid his face and went red.
In 'The ancient castle crumbled', what does 'ancient' probably mean?
Very old.
Amy packed a torch, a map and snacks before setting off at night – what do you predict she will do?
e.g. Go exploring or on an adventure somewhere dark.
Why might a writer put a heading above each section of a fact page?
To show what each part is about so you can find information quickly.
Can you sum up a story you've just read in one sentence?
e.g. 'A boy loses his dog, searches the town and finds it in the park.'
Read a fact page or recipe together and ask your child to find three facts and write them as a short list.
Look at a food packet together and ask your child to find the weight, the cooking time and where it was made.
Use the contents page or index of a non-fiction book to find a page about one animal and read it together.
Ask your child to make a mini fact file (habitat, food, size) about an animal from a book or website.
Read a leaflet or timetable together and ask three questions whose answers are in it, such as 'What time does it open?'
After reading a chapter, take turns to say one thing you liked, waiting until the other person has finished.
Ask 'What would you have done if you were the main character?' and share your own answer too.
Use a 'talking object', like a spoon, so only the person holding it speaks about the book.
When your child gives an opinion about a book, ask 'Why do you think that?' and help them point to the part that shows it.
Ask your child to repeat back one thing you said about the story before adding their own idea.
Add '-ly' to 'happy' – how do you spell it?
happily (change the y to i)
Add '-ation' to 'inform' – what word do you get?
information
Add '-ous' to 'danger' – how do you spell it?
dangerous
Add '-ly' to 'gentle' – how do you spell it?
gently (the -le changes to -ly)
Which prefix makes the opposite of 'appear': un-, dis- or mis-?
dis- – disappear
Which spelling means a part of something: 'peace' or 'piece'?
piece – as in a piece of cake
Spell the word 'break' that means to smash something.
b-r-e-a-k (a 'brake' stops a bike or car)
Which spelling goes in 'I can ___ the birds': 'here' or 'hear'?
hear – you hear with your ear
Which spelling goes in 'The ___ is sunny today': 'weather' or 'whether'?
weather
Spell the word 'meet' that means to get together with someone.
m-e-e-t ('meat' is food)
Spell 'February'.
F-e-b-r-u-a-r-y (don't forget the first r)
Spell 'separate'.
s-e-p-a-r-a-t-e (there's 'a rat' in separate)
Spell 'believe'.
b-e-l-i-e-v-e (never believe a lie)
Spell 'library'.
l-i-b-r-a-r-y
Spell 'favourite'.
f-a-v-o-u-r-i-t-e
Add the apostrophe: 'the girls bags' (more than one girl).
the girls' bags
Add the apostrophe: 'the childrens toys'.
the children's toys
Write 'the coats belonging to the boys' using an apostrophe.
the boys' coats
Write 'the hats belonging to the men' using an apostrophe.
the men's hats
Is 'the dogs' bowls' about one dog or more than one?
More than one – the apostrophe comes after the s.
In a dictionary, which comes first: 'bread' or 'brick'?
bread – e comes before i
Which comes first in a dictionary: 'shell' or 'sheep'?
sheep – look at the fourth letter: e comes before l
Put these in dictionary order: cup, cat, clock.
cat, clock, cup
Which first three letters would you look up to check the spelling of 'tricycle'?
t-r-i
Would 'zebra' be near the front, middle or back of a dictionary?
Right at the back – z is the last letter.
Say a short sentence such as 'Amy heard a strange noise in February.' and ask your child to write it from memory, then check it together.
Say a sentence once, have your child repeat it aloud, then ask them to write it without hearing it again.
Dictate a question such as 'Where is the boys' football?' and check the question mark and apostrophe together.
Dictate a sentence with speech, such as "Can we go now?" asked Mia., and check the inverted commas together.
After a dictation, ask your child to underline any word they're unsure of and check it in a dictionary.
Practise a row each of 'in', 'an' and 'un', using the diagonal join from the bottom of one letter up to the next.
Practise horizontal joins from the top of letters like o, v and w by writing rows of 'oo', 'ow' and 'vi'.
Write a row each of 'the' and 'ing' in joined handwriting, keeping the letters the same size.
Ask your child which letters their school leaves unjoined (often capitals and sometimes letters with tails), then write a few words using them.
Copy a short sentence in joined handwriting together, then circle the neatest join.
Write a sentence on lined paper and check that tall letters and tails don't touch the lines of writing above or below.
Look at a written word together and check that the downstrokes all lean the same way and are evenly spaced.
Write a row of 'ill' or 'mum' and pick the neatest one together, saying why it's best.
Ask your child to copy the shopping list neatly, leaving a finger space between words.
Write the same sentence slowly and then a little faster, and compare which is still easy to read.
Read a short story or fact page together and talk about how it starts, what happens in the middle and how it ends.
Jot down story ideas on scrap paper together: who, where, the problem and how it gets solved.
Make a quick three-box plan for beginning, middle and end, using notes or small drawings.
Collect five exciting words or phrases from a book you're reading to use in your child's own writing.
Before writing a letter or instructions, look at a real one at home and point out how it's set out.
Ask your child to say each sentence aloud before writing it, changing it if it doesn't sound right.
Describe a setting together, such as a stormy beach, using sight, sound and smell words, then write two sentences about it.
Invent a character together – their name, looks, likes and dislikes – then write a short paragraph about them.
Write a short fact page about a hobby with a heading and two sub-headings, grouping the facts into paragraphs.
Act out a quick conversation between two characters, then write it down as dialogue.
Make this clearer: 'Sam and Ben went to the park and he fell over.'
e.g. 'Sam and Ben went to the park and Ben fell over.'
Improve this so it doesn't repeat 'Mia': 'Mia had a dog. Mia's dog was brown. Mia loved the dog.'
e.g. 'Mia had a brown dog and she loved it.'
Which is better: 'The cake was nice' or 'The cake was delicious'?
'Delicious' – it's more exact and interesting.
Fix the tense: 'Yesterday I go to the shop and bought milk.'
Yesterday I went to the shop and bought milk.
What is one thing that went well, and one thing to improve, in the last thing you wrote?
e.g. 'I used good describing words, but I need more full stops.'
Spot the mistakes: 'i went to the park on monday.'
'I' and 'Monday' need capital letters.
Spot the spelling mistake: 'We had a suprise party.'
surprise – s-u-r-p-r-i-s-e
What's missing: 'Where are my shoes'
A question mark at the end.
Spot the mistake: 'Their going to the beach tomorrow.'
'Their' should be 'They're' (they are).
Spot the spelling mistake: 'I must remeber my bag.'
remember – r-e-m-e-m-b-e-r
Ask your child to read their own story to the family, pausing at full stops and commas.
Practise reading one sentence in a happy, a scared and a whispery voice, then choose which fits best.
Record your child reading their writing on a phone and listen back together to check it's clear.
Ask your child to read a question from their writing so their voice rises at the end.
Ask your child to read speech in a different voice from the narrator, as if performing to an audience.
Join with 'because': 'I took my coat. It was raining.'
I took my coat because it was raining.
Finish the sentence: 'We played outside although…'
e.g. 'We played outside although it was cold.'
Which uses the present perfect: 'I ate my lunch' or 'I have eaten my lunch'?
I have eaten my lunch
Add a fronted adverbial: '___, the cat crept across the garden.'
e.g. 'Silently, …' or 'After dinner, …'
Say 'a' or 'an' before each: orange, banana, hour.
an orange, a banana, an hour
Where does the comma go: 'Later that day Mia found a key.'
After 'day': Later that day, Mia found a key.
Punctuate: Sam said I'm hungry
Sam said, "I'm hungry."
Punctuate: Where are you going asked Amy
"Where are you going?" asked Amy.
Add the apostrophe: 'the teachers cars' (more than one teacher).
the teachers' cars
Where does the comma go: 'Under the bridge the troll waited.'
After 'bridge': Under the bridge, the troll waited.
What is the preposition in 'The ball rolled under the table'?
under
What are the punctuation marks around spoken words called?
Inverted commas (also called speech marks).
Which word is the pronoun in 'Ben dropped it on the floor'?
it
What is the determiner in 'a red bike'?
a
Name some words in the same word family as 'solve'.
e.g. solution, solver, dissolve
What comes next: 4, 8, 12, 16, …?
Count in 50s: 0, 50, 100, 150, … what comes next?
What is 100 more than 347?
Count in 8s: 8, 16, 24, 32, … what comes next?
What is 10 less than 405?
In 352, what is the 5 worth?
50 (5 tens)
In 714, what is the 7 worth?
700 (7 hundreds)
How many hundreds, tens and ones are in 608?
6 hundreds, 0 tens and 8 ones
What number has 4 hundreds, 2 tens and 9 ones?
What number is 3 hundreds and 15 ones?
Which is bigger, 289 or 298?
Is 506 bigger or smaller than 560?
Smaller (506 < 560)
Put in order, smallest first: 431, 413, 341.
Which is the smallest: 709, 790 or 97?
Put in order, largest first: 625, 652, 256, 562.
What number is 2 hundreds squares, 3 tens sticks and 4 ones cubes?
What number is exactly halfway along a 0 to 100 number line?
Is 680 closer to 600 or 700?
What number is halfway between 300 and 400?
What number is 5 hundreds and 12 tens?
Write four hundred and seven in numerals.
Write 365 in words.
three hundred and sixty-five
Write eight hundred and ninety in numerals.
Write 512 in words.
five hundred and twelve
Write nine hundred and nine in numerals.
Amy has 3 boxes of 100 stickers and 6 loose stickers. How many stickers is that?
306 stickers
A comic costs 250p and a book costs 100p more. How much is the book?
Use the digits 4, 7 and 1 to make the biggest three-digit number you can.
Use the digits 4, 7 and 1 to make the smallest three-digit number you can.
Pencils come in packs of 10. How many packs make 230 pencils?
23 packs
What is 345 + 3?
What is 562 + 30?
What is 418 − 200?
What is 276 + 7?
What is 432 − 50?
Work out 234 + 152 in columns.
Work out 468 − 125 in columns.
Work out 357 + 246 in columns.
Work out 520 − 184 in columns.
Ben has 403 points and loses 167. How many points are left?
236 points
Estimate 198 + 302 by rounding each number to the nearest hundred.
Estimate 412 − 189 by rounding each number to the nearest hundred.
Mia says 245 + 130 = 375. What subtraction would check it?
Is 386 − 142 = 244 right? Check with an addition.
Sam says 503 − 278 = 335. Check with an addition: is he right?
No, 335 + 278 = 613; the answer is 225
Amy ate 35 sweets and has 128 left. How many did she start with?
163 sweets
What is 4 × 6?
What is 8 × 5?
What is 24 ÷ 3?
What is 7 × 8?
What is 72 ÷ 8?
What is 20 × 3?
What is 13 × 4?
What is 24 × 3?
What is 16 × 8?
What is 96 ÷ 3?
A tower is 3 cm tall and another is 4 times as tall. How tall is the second tower?
12 cm
Sweets come in bags of 8. How many bags hold 48 sweets?
6 bags
Mia has 3 tops and 2 skirts. How many different outfits can she make?
6 outfits
A rabbit eats 3 carrots a day. How many carrots does it eat in 2 weeks?
42 carrots
Count on in tenths: 1/10, 2/10, 3/10, … what comes next?
A bar is cut into 10 equal pieces. What fraction is one piece?
1/10 (one tenth)
How many tenths make one whole?
10 tenths
Count back in tenths: 9/10, 8/10, 7/10, … what comes next?
What is 3 ÷ 10 written as a fraction?
What is 1/2 of 10 sweets?
5 sweets
What is 1/3 of 12 sweets?
4 sweets
What is 1/4 of 20p?
5p
What is 2/3 of 15 sweets?
10 sweets
What is 3/4 of 24 cm?
18 cm
What fraction is exactly halfway between 0 and 1?
How many quarters make one whole?
4 quarters
A 0 to 1 number line is split into 4 equal parts. What is the first mark?
On a 0 to 1 number line in fifths, what comes after 2/5?
Count in thirds: 1/3, 2/3, … what comes next?
3/3 (one whole)
How many quarters are the same as one half?
2 quarters (2/4)
Mia eats 4/8 of a pizza and Ben eats 1/2 of the same size pizza. Who eats more?
Neither, they eat the same amount
What is 1/4 + 2/4?
What is 3/5 − 1/5?
What is 2/7 + 4/7?
What is 7/8 − 3/8?
Sam eats 2/6 of a cake and Amy eats 3/6. What fraction is left?
Which is bigger, 1/2 or 1/4?
Which is bigger, 3/5 or 2/5?
Which is bigger, 1/3 or 1/5?
Put in order, smallest first: 1/4, 1/2, 1/8.
Put in order, smallest first: 5/9, 2/9, 7/9.
A pizza is cut into 8 equal slices and Ben eats 3. What fraction has he eaten?
Amy has 20p and spends 1/4 of it. How much does she spend?
5p
Sam eats 2/5 of a bar of chocolate. What fraction is left?
There are 12 sweets and 1/3 of them are red. How many are not red?
8 sweets
A ribbon is 30 cm long and Mia cuts off 3/10 of it. How much is left?
21 cm
How many millimetres are in 1 cm?
10 mm
What is 35 cm + 48 cm?
83 cm
How many grams are in 1 kg?
A jug holds 1 litre and you pour out 350 ml. How much is left?
650 ml
Which is longer, 1 m 20 cm or 125 cm?
125 cm (1 m 20 cm is 120 cm)
A square has sides of 3 cm. What is its perimeter?
12 cm
A rectangle is 5 cm long and 2 cm wide. What is its perimeter?
14 cm
A triangle has sides of 4 cm, 5 cm and 6 cm. What is its perimeter?
15 cm
A rectangle is 10 cm long and 7 cm wide. What is its perimeter?
34 cm
A square has a perimeter of 20 cm. How long is each side?
5 cm
You pay £1 for something that costs 60p. How much change do you get?
What is £1.20 add 50p?
Sweets cost 45p and a drink costs 80p. How much is that altogether?
A comic costs £2.35 and you pay with £5. How much change do you get?
Mia buys an apple for 75p and a sandwich for £1.50 and pays with £5. How much change does she get?
What number is the Roman numeral V?
What number is the Roman numeral IX?
What is 15:00 on a 12-hour clock?
Write 7:30 p.m. using the 24-hour clock.
The hour hand is just past VIII and the minute hand points to VI. What time is it?
Half past eight (8:30)
Is 9 o'clock in the morning a.m. or p.m.?
a.m.
What do we call 12 o'clock in the middle of the day?
Noon (midday)
Which is longer, 90 seconds or 1 minute?
90 seconds
The minute hand points 3 small marks past the 4. How many minutes past the hour is it?
23 minutes past
Which is longer, 2 hours or 100 minutes?
2 hours (120 minutes)
How many seconds are in 1 minute?
60 seconds
How many days are in April?
30 days
How many days are in a year that is not a leap year?
365 days
How many days are in February in a leap year?
29 days
How many seconds are in 3 minutes?
180 seconds
A film starts at 2:00 and ends at 3:30. How long is it?
1 hour 30 minutes
Sam reads from 4:10 to 4:35. How long does he read for?
25 minutes
Amy runs a race in 48 seconds and Ben takes 55 seconds. How much faster is Amy?
7 seconds
A cake goes in the oven at 10:45 and bakes for 40 minutes. What time does it come out?
A train leaves at 13:50 and arrives at 15:15. How long is the journey?
1 hour 25 minutes
How many faces does a cube have?
6 faces
How many corners (vertices) does a cube have?
8 vertices
What 3-D shape is a tin of soup?
A cylinder
How many faces does a square-based pyramid have?
5 faces
How many edges does a cuboid have?
12 edges
How many angles does a triangle have?
3 angles
How many angles does a pentagon have?
5 angles
You face the door and turn until you face the door again. What turn is that?
A whole turn
You face north and make a quarter turn clockwise. Which way do you face now?
East
You face north and make a three-quarter turn clockwise. Which way do you face now?
West
How many right angles does a square have?
4 right angles
How many right angles make a half turn?
2 right angles
Three right angles make what fraction of a whole turn?
Three quarters of a turn
At 3 o'clock, is the angle between the clock hands a right angle?
Yes, it is a right angle
At 1 o'clock, is the angle between the clock hands bigger or smaller than a right angle?
Smaller than a right angle
Is a flagpole standing up straight horizontal or vertical?
Vertical
Is the top of a table horizontal or vertical?
Horizontal
What do we call two straight lines that never meet, like train tracks?
Parallel lines
What do we call two lines that meet at a right angle?
Perpendicular lines
How many pairs of parallel sides does a rectangle have?
2 pairs
In a pictogram, one smiley stands for 2 children. How many children do 4 smileys show?
8 children
In a pictogram, one circle stands for 4 sweets. How many sweets do 2 and a half circles show?
10 sweets
A bar chart scale goes up in 10s. A bar stops halfway between 30 and 40. What does it show?
A table shows 12 cats and 9 dogs. How many pets is that altogether?
21 pets
In a pictogram, one picture stands for 10 cars. How many pictures show 60 cars?
6 pictures
Red got 8 votes and blue got 5. How many more votes did red get?
3 more votes
In a pictogram, one picture stands for 2 books. Monday has 4 pictures and Tuesday has 6. How many more books on Tuesday?
4 more books
A bar chart shows 30 apples and 45 bananas. How many fewer apples are there?
15 fewer apples
A table shows 25 children in Class A, 18 in Class B and 22 in Class C. How many children altogether?
65 children
A table shows 40 sweets sold on Monday and 25 on Tuesday. Each sweet costs 2p. How much more money was made on Monday?
The prefix 'auto' means 'self', so what does 'autobiography' mean?
A life story written by the person themselves.
The root 'aqua' means water; can you think of a word that uses it?
e.g. aquarium, aquatic, aqueduct.
What does the prefix 'mis' do to 'understand' in 'misunderstand'?
It means 'wrongly' – to understand something wrongly.
'Transport' and 'transfer' both start with 'trans'; what does 'trans' mean?
Across or from one place to another.
What do 'telephone', 'television' and 'telescope' have in common in meaning?
They all start with 'tele', meaning far or at a distance.
Choose a type of book your child doesn't usually read – a myth, a poem collection or a non-fiction book – and read a chapter or section together.
Ask your child to 'sell' you a book they've enjoyed in one minute, giving at least two reasons why you should read it.
Pick a short poem and help your child learn the first verse by heart, saying a line at a time.
Read a short scene or poem aloud together, trying different voices, volumes and pauses to make the meaning clear.
Compare two stories you both know (such as two fairy tales or legends) and talk about what themes or patterns they share.
'Mia slammed the door and stomped upstairs without a word.' How is Mia feeling, and how do you know?
e.g. Angry or upset – slamming the door and stomping show it, and not speaking suggests she's cross.
'Ben kept glancing at the clock and tapping his foot.' What can you infer about Ben?
e.g. He is impatient, nervous or waiting for something – the glancing and tapping show it.
In a story, what does it mean to summarise a chapter?
To give the main ideas in a few sentences, leaving out small details.
'The sky darkened and the wind began to howl.' What might happen next?
e.g. A storm might start – the dark sky and howling wind are clues.
If you meet a word you don't know in a book, what can you do to work out its meaning?
e.g. Read the sentence around it for clues, look for a root word you know, or check a dictionary.
Is 'The classroom was a zoo' a simile or a metaphor?
A metaphor – it says the classroom IS a zoo, without 'like' or 'as'.
Is 'Her smile was as bright as the sun' a simile or a metaphor?
A simile – it compares using 'as'.
What is personification in 'The wind whispered through the trees'?
Giving the wind a human action – whispering.
Why might an author write 'the waves crashed and smashed' instead of 'the waves moved'?
e.g. The stronger verbs (and onomatopoeia) help the reader hear and feel how powerful the sea is.
What does 'He has a heart of stone' really mean?
He is unkind or doesn't show feelings – it's figurative, not literal.
Fact or opinion: 'London is the capital of England.'
Fact – it can be checked and proved.
Fact or opinion: 'Football is the best sport in the world.'
Opinion – it's what someone thinks, not something that can be proved.
Fact or opinion: 'Water boils at 100°C at sea level.'
Fact.
Which word in 'Sadly, the delicious cake was eaten' shows an opinion?
'Delicious' (and 'sadly') – they show what the writer thinks.
Can you turn the fact 'Dogs have four legs' into an opinion?
e.g. 'Dogs are the most loyal pets you can have.'
Find a non-fiction book or leaflet at home and give your child three questions to answer by scanning it for the facts.
Ask your child to use the contents page and index of a non-fiction book to find a fact on a topic you choose.
Read a short news article together and ask your child to note the 'who, what, where, when, why' as bullet points.
Ask your child to turn facts from a recipe, timetable or leaflet into a simple table or chart.
Choose an animal and have your child find five facts from a reference book, then present them to you as a mini fact file.
After reading a chapter together, each share one thing you liked and one question you have about it.
Ask your child whether they agree with a character's choice, then gently give a different view and see how they respond politely.
Practise phrases for disagreeing kindly, such as 'I see what you mean, but…' or 'I'd add that…', while talking about a book.
Take turns building on each other's ideas about a story, starting each turn with 'Yes, and…'.
Read a short poem aloud and talk about what you each think it means, comparing your ideas.
Ask your child to give a two-minute talk about a book they've read, using a few notes on a card.
Hold a mini debate on a question from a story, such as 'Was the main character right?', with each person giving two reasons.
Ask your child to jot three bullet-point notes about a chapter, then explain the chapter to you using only those notes.
Play 'stay on topic': your child talks for one minute about a book and you buzz if they wander off the subject.
Ask your child to present a non-fiction topic they've read about to the family, standing up and speaking clearly.
Ask 'Which was the best character in the book you're reading, and why?' and encourage answers using 'because'.
Give a simple statement, such as 'Homework should be banned', and ask your child to give two reasons for and one against.
When your child gives an opinion about a story, ask 'What in the text makes you think that?'
Choose between two films, games or books together, each giving reasons, and see who persuades whom.
Practise using linking phrases like 'firstly', 'furthermore' and 'however' when your child explains a view.
What do you get when you add -ous to 'vice'?
Vicious – the 'shus' sound is spelt -cious.
Spell the adjective from 'ambition'.
Ambitious (-tious, because the root ends in -tion).
Which is right: 'officail', 'official' or 'offitial'?
Official (-cial after a vowel).
Does 'reasonable' or 'reasonible' have the correct ending?
Reasonable – 'reason' is a complete word, so -able is usually used.
Add -ence or -ance: 'obedi___'.
Obedience (from obedient).
Which letter is silent in 'knight'?
The 'k' (and the 'gh' is silent too).
Which letter is silent in 'solemn'?
The 'n'.
Which letter is silent in 'psalm'?
The 'p' (and the 'l').
Spell the word for the joint in the middle of your leg.
Knee.
Can you name a word with a silent 'w'?
e.g. write, wrong, wrist, answer, sword.
'I need some ___ on my homework.' Advice or advise?
Advice (the noun); 'advise' is the verb.
What is the difference between 'stationary' and 'stationery'?
Stationary means not moving; stationery is paper, pens and envelopes.
'Ice cream is my favourite ___.' Desert or dessert?
Dessert (a sweet course; a desert is a dry, sandy place).
'The loud noise will ___ my concentration.' Affect or effect?
Affect (the verb); 'effect' is usually the noun.
'___ coat is this?' Who's or whose?
Whose (who's means 'who is' or 'who has').
How do you spell 'necessary'?
N-E-C-E-S-S-A-R-Y (one c, double s).
How do you spell 'embarrass'?
E-M-B-A-R-R-A-S-S (double r, double s).
How do you spell 'definite'?
D-E-F-I-N-I-T-E (it contains 'finite').
'Sign' has a silent g – how does that help you spell 'signature'?
The g is heard in 'signature', and it comes from the same root, 'sign'.
How do you spell 'rhythm'?
R-H-Y-T-H-M.
Pick three tricky words from your child's reading and ask them to check the meanings in a dictionary.
Race to find a given word in a dictionary – whoever finds it first reads out its definition.
Ask your child to spell a word they're unsure of, then check it in the dictionary together.
Find a word with more than one meaning in the dictionary (such as 'bark' or 'bat') and talk about each meaning.
Open the dictionary at a random page, choose an unfamiliar word, and challenge your child to use it in a sentence today.
Which comes first in a dictionary: 'stamp' or 'stair'?
Stair (sta-i comes before sta-m).
Which comes first: 'present' or 'pressure'?
Present (pres-e comes before pres-s).
Put in dictionary order: 'chair', 'chain', 'chalk'.
Chain, chair, chalk.
Which comes first: 'thorough' or 'though'?
Thorough (thor comes before thou).
You can't spell 'necessary' – which first letters would you look up?
N-E-C-E, then scan down until you find it.
Give a synonym for 'big' that sounds more powerful.
e.g. enormous, gigantic, immense, colossal.
What is an antonym of 'generous'?
e.g. mean, selfish, stingy.
Give three synonyms for 'said'.
e.g. whispered, replied, announced, muttered.
Is 'ancient' a synonym or an antonym of 'modern'?
An antonym (opposite).
Replace 'nice' in 'We had a nice day' with a stronger word.
e.g. wonderful, delightful, memorable, enjoyable.
Ask your child to copy a short poem in their neatest joined handwriting and then read it back to check it's legible.
Time your child writing a sentence neatly for one minute, then see if they can write more next time while keeping it readable.
Ask your child which pen or pencil suits a task best, such as a birthday card, a quick note or labelling a diagram.
Write a shopping list quickly in print, then a thank-you note in careful joined writing, and talk about the difference.
Practise tricky joins like 'br', 'ow' and 'ss' in a row of five, checking letters sit evenly on the line.
Before your child writes something, ask 'Who is it for and why are you writing it?' and choose the right form together.
Read a short example of the type of writing they're doing (such as a letter or report) and spot features they could borrow.
Draw a quick mind map or spider diagram together to collect ideas for a story or piece of writing.
Think of a character from a book you know and list how the author shows what they're like, then plan your own character the same way.
Look up two or three facts together on a topic before your child writes a non-fiction piece about it.
Ask your child to describe a room at home in three sentences to create a spooky or cosy atmosphere.
Write a short conversation between two characters where the dialogue shows how each one feels.
Read a paragraph from a newspaper or book and ask your child to sum it up in one sentence (a précis).
Practise linking paragraphs using phrases such as 'Later that day', 'On the other hand' or 'As a result'.
Turn a short piece of writing into a mini information page using a heading, subheadings and bullet points.
Fix the tense: 'Yesterday I walk to the park and played football.'
Yesterday I walked to the park and played football.
Which is correct: 'The children was playing' or 'The children were playing'?
The children were playing (plural subject, plural verb).
Make this more formal: 'Hi, can you send me the stuff?'
e.g. 'Dear Sir or Madam, please could you send me the items?'
Which is correct: 'Each of the boys has a bag' or 'Each of the boys have a bag'?
Each of the boys has a bag ('each' is singular).
Improve 'The dog went down the road' with a better verb.
e.g. The dog bounded/trotted/raced down the road.
Find the mistake: 'I recieved a letter.'
Received – 'i before e except after c'.
Find the mistake: 'Its raining today.'
It's – it needs an apostrophe because it means 'it is'.
Find the mistake: 'The dogs bone was buried.'

Find the mistake: 'Where are you going asked Amy.'

Find the mistake: 'We went to the restraunt for dinner.'
Restaurant.
Ask your child to read aloud a story or poem they've written, changing their voice for different characters.
Practise reading one line of your child's writing in a happy, scary and sad voice and talk about which fits best.
Help your child add one or two gestures or movements to their performance to show what's happening.
Record your child reading their writing on a phone and listen back together to check it's clear and well paced.
Have your child perform their writing to the family, remembering to look up and pause at full stops.
Change into the passive voice: 'The cat chased the mouse.'
The mouse was chased by the cat.
Which word in 'Sam might go to the party' shows possibility?
'Might' – a modal verb.
Add a relative clause: 'My aunt ___ lives in Wales is visiting.'
e.g. My aunt, who lives in Wales, is visiting.
Which sentence uses the subjunctive: 'If I was you…' or 'If I were you…'?
'If I were you…'
Which sentence uses the present perfect: 'She ate lunch' or 'She has eaten lunch'?
She has eaten lunch.
Where does the comma go to change the meaning: 'Let's eat Grandma'?
Let's eat, Grandma.
What is the difference between 'man-eating shark' and 'man eating shark'?
The hyphen shows the shark eats people; without it, it could be a man eating shark.
Add brackets: 'My brother who is eight loves football.'
My brother (who is eight) loves football.
Join with a semi-colon: 'It was raining. We stayed inside.'
It was raining; we stayed inside.
Where does the colon go: 'I packed three things a torch, a map and a coat.'
After 'things': I packed three things: a torch, a map and a coat.
What is a relative clause?
A type of clause that adds information about a noun, often starting with who, which, where, when, whose or that.
What is the subject in 'The tall boy kicked the ball'?
The tall boy.
What is the difference between active and passive voice?
Active: the subject does the action. Passive: the subject has the action done to it.
What is a modal verb? Give an example.
A verb that shows how likely or necessary something is, e.g. can, could, might, should, will, must.
What is cohesion in writing?
How sentences and paragraphs link together, e.g. using pronouns, conjunctions and adverbials.
